The Cretaceous Period. From one hundred and forty-five to sixty-six million years ago, the Cretaceous saw the final flourishing of dinosaurs alongside the rise of flowering plants, which came to dominate the landscape. Ceratopsians and ankylosaurs diversified, and Tyrannosaurus rex stalked the Late Cretaceous. The period ended abruptly sixty-six million years ago with an asteroid impact that erased dinosaurs and reshaped Earth's biosphere. The name comes from the chalk deposits, called creta in Latin, that characterise the rocks of this period.

Flowering plants radiated dramatically during the Cretaceous, becoming the dominant flora and providing new food sources for dinosaurs. Ceratopsian dinosaurs like Triceratops evolved elaborate horns and frills, possibly for display and combat. Ankylosaurs—armored herbivores with bony clubs on their tails—diversified during the Late Cretaceous. Tyrannosaurus rex, the apex predator of the Late Cretaceous, evolved sophisticated hunting behaviours and sensory abilities.

The extinction event known as the K-Pg extinction struck sixty-six million years ago, triggered by a massive asteroid impact in what is now Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula. It killed roughly seventy-five percent of all species, including all non-avian dinosaurs. Birds, which are avian dinosaurs, survived the extinction, as did mammals, which remained small and opportunistic in the shadow of dinosaurs.

The Cretaceous follows the Jurassic Period, the previous age of dinosaur dominance, and precedes the Cenozoic Era, when mammals inherited the Earth.
